messages.author: ee490f1373633c05
messages.subject: Definition of "fast" vs "slow" parameters
parts:
Hello all,

At present, STAN samples all parameters at every iteration.

In some cases, it may be useful to partition the parameters into "fast" and "slow" subsets, where fast parameters are quick to update, whilst slow parameters are not.  The logic here is that you might only update the slow parameters every N iterations.

As an example, consider Gaussian Process Regression, where a training set is used to make predictions for a prediction set.  Full Bayes (and therefore full MCMC) is slow because the hyperparameters are expensive to optimise/sample from.  One alternative to this is to use empirical Bayes, whereby I set the hyperparameters to their maximum a posteriori (MAP) values, and then just sample from the GP as desired. 

I see two possibilities here:
1) STAN could be programmed to optimise some parameters (eg hyperparameters) whilst sampling others.  I don't know how difficult such a mixed implementation would be, but certainly there is an element of Gibbs-like sampling here (the sampled parameters will be sampled conditional on the values of the optmised parameters); or
2) You might only update the hyperparameters every N iterations.  Then, you can get significantly more samples from the "fast" predictions.

The second case is effectively a half-way house between empirical Bayes and MCMC - you get somewhat more realistic confidence intervals, and faster running times than full MCMC, assuming that your hyperparameters are close to the MAP values.

Is something like this interesting? Is it feasible?  For the speed gain to be realised here, STAN would need to know not to calculate the derivatives of "slow" parameters at specified iterations.

Thoughts?

Thanks
Julian

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Definition of "fast" vs "slow" parameters
parts:
Hi, I’m a bit confused.  You say that in variational Bayes, you set the hyperparameters to their maximum a posteriori (MAP) values.  But that’s not how I thought variational Bayes worked.  In my impression, in variational Bayes there is a distributional approximation to the hyperparameters; they are not simply set at point values.  So I think there’s something I’m missing here.

Speaking more generally about how Stan is structured:  Currently it only allows jumping through the full space of parameters.  But we are planning to implement a partition of parameter space so that it can jump on one set of parameters with the others set at fixed values.

A

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Definition of "fast" vs "slow" parameters
parts:
Getting more samples by freezing more expensive hyper parameters does absolutely 
nothing for you as p (fast | slow) != p (fast) = \int dslow p(fast, slow).  In particular,
the conditional distribution drastically underestimates the true marginal uncertainty
of the fast parameters.  There are various ways to estimate p(fast | slow) but none
of them can get around the ultimate lack of utility of the conditional distribution for
inference.

P.S. STAN should be Stan
